title: Stolen Pets, Broken Trust: Vietnam’s Dog Trade Faces Public Reckoning
excerpt: Pet theft turns family loss into a safety crisis. Recent cases and rabies data strengthen Vietnam’s locally led call to end the trade.
body_html:
The Bottom Line

Stolen dogs leave families grieving and expose failures across an unregulated supply chain. Recent convictions, cruelty enforcement, and rabies outbreaks show why Vietnam needs safer animal control and a locally led end to the trade, supported by 95% of Vietnamese people.

Key Findings

A September court case shows how pet theft feeds the trade

On 9 September 2026, a court in Tây Ninh sentenced three people for stealing and selling dogs. Nguyễn Thanh Xuân received four years in prison, Phan Trung Chánh received two years, and Đoàn Thị Lương received one year. Authorities reported that the group transported 19 dogs when caught and that the case involved more than 1.6 tonnes of dogs.

These numbers represent more than an illegal transaction. Each stolen pet can mean a family searching streets, checking cameras, and losing a trusted companion without answers. The case also shows how theft can connect household dogs to commercial channels.

Cruelty enforcement is moving closer to public view

Authorities in Đà Lạt fined a man VND2 million on 4 September 2026 after a video showed him beating an Alaska Malamute at Lam Vien Square. The case received police attention after public reporting, while Decree 211/2026 sets fines of VND1 million to VND3 million for beating or cruelly mistreating animals.

Public accountability matters because cruelty often stays hidden during capture, transport, and sale. Clear penalties give families and witnesses a route to report abuse before harm escalates.

Rabies makes unsafe dog handling a public-safety issue

On 7 September 2026, health authorities reported that a dog in Đắk Lắk tested positive for rabies after attacking four people. National reporting recorded 164 animal rabies outbreaks across 129 communes, wards, and townships in 22 provinces and cities by 3 September, with 51 human deaths since the start of 2026.

Hanoi CDC guidance warned people not to slaughter, eat, or use products from animals suspected of rabies. Unsafe capture and transport create risks for handlers, families, consumers, and communities.

Vietnam has tightening controls, but no national dog-meat ban

September 2026 measures focused on food inspection, veterinary hygiene, animal-product quarantine, and broader food-safety reform. Available reporting does not confirm passage of a national law banning dog meat, leaving a gap between public concern and national policy.

The supply chain remains especially difficult to oversee because Vietnam has zero registered dog slaughterhouses. Closing that gap requires locally led policy, stronger pet identification, vaccination, humane shelter systems, and enforcement against theft.

Local support gives reform a clear mandate

A 2021 survey found that 95% of Vietnamese people supported ending the dog meat trade. That majority places reform in Vietnamese hands: families, veterinarians, local authorities, health workers, and communities can protect animals while reducing rabies and food-safety risks.

Lucky, a nine-year-old Vietnamese Ta dog and beloved family companion, represents the dogs behind these statistics. Ending theft and cruelty protects companions like Lucky and supports safer communities.

Also Worth Noting

  • Đà Nẵng builds a holding facility — On 10 September 2026, authorities began inspections and required owners to register, vaccinate, leash, or confine dogs and cats.
  • Emergency vaccination — Cù Lao Dung commune reported 550 emergency doses and more than 1,300 dog and cat vaccinations during 2026.
  • Đồng Tháp raises prevention targets — Authorities required vaccination for at least 80% of eligible dogs and cats amid nationwide rabies outbreaks.
  • Regulation remains incomplete — September discussions addressed veterinary medicines and slaughter inspection, not a specific national dog-meat ban.
  • Public support is measurable — The 95% support figure strengthens a locally led roadmap to end the trade by 2030.

Take Action: Sign the petition to support Vietnam's roadmap toward eliminating the dog meat trade by 2030.
